1	# Versal SAR Backprojection Design
2	
3	## Introduction
4	
5	**NOTE: This repository should not be cloned directly! Instead, follow the
6	instructions in the
7	[versal-manifest](https://github.com/nasa-jpl/versal-manifest) repo to collect
8	all the necessary repos required for building this design.**
9	
10	This repo contains the source code for implementing backprojection onto the AMD
11	Versal ACAP, along with a makefile to help build the project and various helper
12	scripts to help flash the project for the Versal target.
13	
14	The repo folder hierarchy contains the following:
15	
16	Directory                     | Contents
17	------------------------------|-----------
18	design/aie                    | Source code for AIE engine on Versal
19	design/exec_scripts           | Scripts that gets transferred to Versal ARM to execute the design
20	design/host                   | Source code for the ARM Cortex-A72 on Versal
21	design/pl                     | Source code for the FPGA on Versal
22	design/profiling_cfgs         | Config that gets transferred to Versal ARM describing various setting of how the design should be ran
23	design/system_cfgs            | Provides information to compiler when compiling the entire design
24	design/test_data              | Test data for slowtime and range compression samples
25	design/vivado_metrics_scripts | Scripts for executing various metrics (power, resource utilization, etc.) for compiled design
26	design/common.h               | Configurations for the design used throughout the entire application
27	helper_scripts                | Helper scripts used to help setup your environment variables and flash the applications on the Versal
28	Makefile                      | Makefile to build out entire project
29	doc                           | Design documentation
30	
31	### Git LFS Installation
32	
33	This repo uses Git LFS for its data input files. In order to use Git LFS,
34	you'll need to download and install a new program that's separate from Git.
35	
36	1. Install git-lfs via your package manager. Ex: `sudo apt install git-lfs`. 
37	Alternatively, you can navigate to [git-lfs.com](https://git-lfs.com/) and 
38	click Download.
39	2. `cd versal-sar-backprojection-design`
40	3. `git lfs install`
41	4. `git lfs pull`
42	
43	### Helper Scripts
44	
45	The various helper scripts in `versal-sar-backprojection-design` repo are summarized below: 
46	
47	- `1_copy_tftpboot_files.sh` - Copies TFTP boot files from the Yocto build into your tftpboot directory. Adjust script as needed for your environment.
48	- `2_copy_nfs_files` - Untars the rootfs that was generated from the Yocto build into your NFS directory. Adjust script as needed for your environment.
49	- `3_copy_app_files` - Copies the application design files into your NFS directory at `/home/root/app`. Adjust script as needed for your environment.
50	- `create_dts.tcl` - Create a starting DTS template for Versal built from your generated XSA in the Versal application design project. Adjust DTS as needed.
51	- `env_setup.sh` - Script to source to set environment variables for your system. Adjust script as needed for your environment.
52	- `flash_bootbin_xsct.tcl` - Flashes the `BOOT.BIN` generated from the Versal application design project over JTAG to Versal.
53	
54	## Building the Project
55	
56	After fetching the required dependencies for this design (as shown in the
57	[versal-manifest](https://github.com/nasa-jpl/versal-manifest) repo), the
58	different components of the design can be built with the below instructions.
59	
60	### Yocto Build
61	
62	From your workspace root directory:
63	
64	```bash
65	cd versal-yocto-build
66	docker build --build-arg USERNAME=<user_name> --build-arg UID="$(id -u)" -t yocto-img .
67	./docker.run -u <user_name> -s $(pwd)/workspace -i yocto-img /bin/bash
68	
69	# Use <user_name> for the password below
70	sudo chown -R <user_name> workspace
71	
72	source build.sh
73	```
74	
75	Where `<user_name>` is any user name you want to have for inside the container. This 
76	does not need to be your host computer's username.
77	
78	The Yocto build can take an hour or longer to build.
79	
80	### SAR Application Design Build
81	
82	If you just built the Yocto build from the above step, exit out of the docker container
83	with `exit`. 
84	
85	You must export the Yocto SDK so that the design can utilize the correct toolchain and 
86	target OS's sysroot. To do this, execute the following from your workspace root directory:
87	
88	```bash
89	cd versal-yocto-build/workspace/poky/build/tmp/deploy/sdk
90	./poky-glibc-x86_64-jpl-versal-image-cortexa72-cortexa53-vck190-versal-toolchain-5.0.3.sh -d toolchain -y
91	```
92	
93	The above command will install Yocto's SDK into a directory called `toolchain`
94	in the current directory. This allows the design application code to link
95	against the sysroot that Yocto created.
96	
97	Next, you need to make sure the
98	[helper/scripts/env_setup.sh](helper_scripts/env_setup.sh) contains the correct
99	paths to your Xilinx installation.
100	
101	Lastly, build the design application:
102	
103	```bash
104	cd versal-sar-backprojection-design
105	source helper_scripts/env_setup.sh
106	make
107	```
108	
109	NOTE: You can run `make` with additional parameters. Refer to top comment in
110	the [Makefile](Makefile) to see what options are available.
111	
112	## Flashing Project to Versal Hardware
113	
114	At this point, you should have everything built from the previous section.
115	
116	Although it is possible to place everything onto an SD card, the recommended
117	way to put the OS and application on the hardware during development is over
118	JTAG and Ethernet using Tiny File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) and Network File
119	System (NFS). This gives the user the most amount of control when configuring
120	the system.
121	
122	### Network File System (NFS)
123	
124	NFS facilitates transfer of file over the network. In this case, we are using
125	it to transfer the entire rootfs created by the Yocto build over the network to
126	the Linux kernel running on the Versal. If you do not have NFS on your host
127	machine, you can install it with `sudo apt install nfs-kernel-server`.
128	
129	You will need to modify your `/etc/exports` file. Depending on your desired NFS
130	configuration and IP address, you may have a diffrent setup. An example of the
131	setup could look something like this:
132	
133	```console
134	/nfs/versal/rootfs 192.168.10.0/24(rw,no_root_squash,no_all_squash,crossmnt)
135	```
136	
137	After you edit the `/etc/exports` file, you need to make the file share
138	available and restart the NFS with the following commands:
139	
140	```bash
141	sudo exportfs -a
142	sudo systemctl restart nfs-kernel-server
143	```
144	
145	The [helper_scripts/2_copy_nfs_files.sh](helper_scripts/2_copy_nfs_files.sh)
146	untars the rootfs that was generated from the Yocto build into the NFS
147	directory. **YOU MUST ADJUST THIS FILE AS NEEDED FOR YOUR ENVIRONMENT.** The
148	`2_copy_nfs_files.sh` assumes your NFS directory is `/nfs/versal/rootfs` by
149	default. If you have followed the above NFS configuration, you shouldn't have
150	to modify this file. However, if you have a diffrent NFS configuration, change
151	the `2_copy_nfs_files.sh` script accordingly.
152	
153	**IMPORTANT:** The Linux kernel running on the Versal must have its kernel

# Versal SAR Backprojection Design

## Introduction

**NOTE: This repository should not be cloned directly! Instead, follow the
instructions in the
[versal-manifest](https://github.com/nasa-jpl/versal-manifest) repo to collect
all the necessary repos required for building this design.**

This repo contains the source code for implementing backprojection onto the AMD
Versal ACAP, along with a makefile to help build the project and various helper
scripts to help flash the project for the Versal target.

The repo folder hierarchy contains the following:

Directory                     | Contents
------------------------------|-----------
design/aie                    | Source code for AIE engine on Versal
design/exec_scripts           | Scripts that gets transferred to Versal ARM to execute the design
design/host                   | Source code for the ARM Cortex-A72 on Versal
design/pl                     | Source code for the FPGA on Versal
design/profiling_cfgs         | Config that gets transferred to Versal ARM describing various setting of how the design should be ran
design/system_cfgs            | Provides information to compiler when compiling the entire design
design/test_data              | Test data for slowtime and range compression samples
design/vivado_metrics_scripts | Scripts for executing various metrics (power, resource utilization, etc.) for compiled design
design/common.h               | Configurations for the design used throughout the entire application
helper_scripts                | Helper scripts used to help setup your environment variables and flash the applications on the Versal
Makefile                      | Makefile to build out entire project
doc                           | Design documentation

### Git LFS Installation

This repo uses Git LFS for its data input files. In order to use Git LFS,
you'll need to download and install a new program that's separate from Git.

1. Install git-lfs via your package manager. Ex: `sudo apt install git-lfs`. 
Alternatively, you can navigate to [git-lfs.com](https://git-lfs.com/) and 
click Download.
2. `cd versal-sar-backprojection-design`
3. `git lfs install`
4. `git lfs pull`

### Helper Scripts

The various helper scripts in `versal-sar-backprojection-design` repo are summarized below: 

- `1_copy_tftpboot_files.sh` - Copies TFTP boot files from the Yocto build into your tftpboot directory. Adjust script as needed for your environment.
- `2_copy_nfs_files` - Untars the rootfs that was generated from the Yocto build into your NFS directory. Adjust script as needed for your environment.
- `3_copy_app_files` - Copies the application design files into your NFS directory at `/home/root/app`. Adjust script as needed for your environment.
- `create_dts.tcl` - Create a starting DTS template for Versal built from your generated XSA in the Versal application design project. Adjust DTS as needed.
- `env_setup.sh` - Script to source to set environment variables for your system. Adjust script as needed for your environment.
- `flash_bootbin_xsct.tcl` - Flashes the `BOOT.BIN` generated from the Versal application design project over JTAG to Versal.

## Building the Project

After fetching the required dependencies for this design (as shown in the
[versal-manifest](https://github.com/nasa-jpl/versal-manifest) repo), the
different components of the design can be built with the below instructions.

### Yocto Build

From your workspace root directory:

```bash
cd versal-yocto-build
docker build --build-arg USERNAME=<user_name> --build-arg UID="$(id -u)" -t yocto-img .
./docker.run -u <user_name> -s $(pwd)/workspace -i yocto-img /bin/bash

# Use <user_name> for the password below
sudo chown -R <user_name> workspace

source build.sh
```

Where `<user_name>` is any user name you want to have for inside the container. This 
does not need to be your host computer's username.

The Yocto build can take an hour or longer to build.

### SAR Application Design Build

If you just built the Yocto build from the above step, exit out of the docker container
with `exit`. 

You must export the Yocto SDK so that the design can utilize the correct toolchain and 
target OS's sysroot. To do this, execute the following from your workspace root directory:

```bash
cd versal-yocto-build/workspace/poky/build/tmp/deploy/sdk
./poky-glibc-x86_64-jpl-versal-image-cortexa72-cortexa53-vck190-versal-toolchain-5.0.3.sh -d toolchain -y
```

The above command will install Yocto's SDK into a directory called `toolchain`
in the current directory. This allows the design application code to link
against the sysroot that Yocto created.

Next, you need to make sure the
[helper/scripts/env_setup.sh](helper_scripts/env_setup.sh) contains the correct
paths to your Xilinx installation.

Lastly, build the design application:

```bash
cd versal-sar-backprojection-design
source helper_scripts/env_setup.sh
make
```

NOTE: You can run `make` with additional parameters. Refer to top comment in
the [Makefile](Makefile) to see what options are available.

## Flashing Project to Versal Hardware

At this point, you should have everything built from the previous section.

Although it is possible to place everything onto an SD card, the recommended
way to put the OS and application on the hardware during development is over
JTAG and Ethernet using Tiny File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) and Network File
System (NFS). This gives the user the most amount of control when configuring
the system.

### Network File System (NFS)

NFS facilitates transfer of file over the network. In this case, we are using
it to transfer the entire rootfs created by the Yocto build over the network to
the Linux kernel running on the Versal. If you do not have NFS on your host
machine, you can install it with `sudo apt install nfs-kernel-server`.

You will need to modify your `/etc/exports` file. Depending on your desired NFS
configuration and IP address, you may have a diffrent setup. An example of the
setup could look something like this:

```console
/nfs/versal/rootfs 192.168.10.0/24(rw,no_root_squash,no_all_squash,crossmnt)
```

After you edit the `/etc/exports` file, you need to make the file share
available and restart the NFS with the following commands:

```bash
sudo exportfs -a
sudo systemctl restart nfs-kernel-server
```

The [helper_scripts/2_copy_nfs_files.sh](helper_scripts/2_copy_nfs_files.sh)
untars the rootfs that was generated from the Yocto build into the NFS
directory. **YOU MUST ADJUST THIS FILE AS NEEDED FOR YOUR ENVIRONMENT.** The
`2_copy_nfs_files.sh` assumes your NFS directory is `/nfs/versal/rootfs` by
default. If you have followed the above NFS configuration, you shouldn't have
to modify this file. However, if you have a diffrent NFS configuration, change
the `2_copy_nfs_files.sh` script accordingly.

way is through the pxeboot configuration located at

    - `/nfs/versal/rootfs` - Path to the NFS directory containing the rootfs.
    - `tcp` - Use TCP transport for NFS (more reliable than UDP).
    - `nfsvers=3` - Force NFSv3 (common for embedded roots)
- `ip=192.168.10.2:::255.255.255.0:versal:eth0:bootp`
    - `192.168.10.2` - Versal IP
    - `255.255.255.0` - Netmask
    - `versal` - Hostname the kernel will assign
    - `eth0` - Network interface to bring up early (for fetching NFS root).
    - `bootp` - Autoconfiguration method (accepts off|on|dhcp|bootp|rarp; here it's BOOTP/DHCP-style).

for your networking configuration. The TFTP client (covered in the next
section) is responsible for transfering over the `default-arm-versal` file to
U-Boot so it can utilize these bootargs when launcing the Linux kernel.

### Tiny File Transfer Protocol (TFTP)

TFTP is responsible for transferring the Linux Kernel and [pxeboot file
(default-arm-versal)](helper_scripts/pxelinux.cfg/default-arm-versal) from your
host machine over to the Versal. This README will not cover TFTP installation
and configuration since there are several online tutorials that cover this
process.

The
[helper_scripts/1_copy_tftpboot_files.sh](helper_scripts/1_copy_tftpboot_files.sh)
copies the TFTP boot files from the Yocto build into your host computer's
tftpboot directory. **YOU MUST ADJUST THIS FILE AS NEEDED FOR YOUR
ENVIRONMENT.** The `1_copy_tftpboot_files.sh` assumes your tftp boot directory
is `/tftpboot` by default. If this is not the case, change the
`1_copy_tftpboot_files.sh` script accordingly.

### Application Executable

Once the NFS is setup and you have the design built, you can use the
[helper_script/3_copy_app_files.sh](helper_script/3_copy_app_files.sh) script to
copy the application design files into the `/home/root/app` directory on the
Versal/host NFS. **YOU MUST ADJUST THIS FILE AS NEEDED FOR YOUR ENVIRONMENT.**
The `3_copy_app_files.sh` assumes your NFS directory is `/nfs/versal/rootfs` by
default. If you have followed the above NFS configuration, you shouldn't have
to modify this file. However, if you have a diffrent NFS configuration, change
the `3_copy_app_files.sh` script accordingly.

### Serial Console

Before flashing the design over JTAG, open up a serial console session with the
Versal. The serial console should be accessible via `/dev/ttyUSB3` (although
the serial devices are dynamically assigned and can change). Both minicom and
screen can be used to access it. 

For example:

```console
minicom -D /dev/ttyUSB3

# OR

screen /dev/ttyUSB3 115200
# To quit screen, press `ctrl+a` then `k` to quit. To detach from screen press `ctrl+a` then `d`. To re-attach to running screen run: `screen -r`
```

The "System Controller" also has a serial console on a separate port that will
start printing boot messages immediately upon power-up. When finished booting,
it will print a link for accessing the web application called "BEAM".

Upon the first time flashing over JTAG, all serial console ports should be
displayed in order to know which serial device port belongs to the Linux
application that will boot.

### JTAG

The
[helper_scripts/flash_bootbin_xsct.tcl](helper_scripts/flash_bootbin_xsct.tcl)
script can be used to flash `BOOT.BIN` into Versal over JTAG. The following
command to execute this TCL script is the following:

```console
cd versal-sar-backprojection-design
xsct ./helper_scripts/flash_bootbin_xsct.tcl
```

Check the serial console to see JTAG/U-Boot/Linux messages.

IMPORTANT: If you are not using a DHCP server for within your network
configuration, you will need to interrupt U-Boot in the serial console by
pressing "enter" (or `ctrl+c`) while it is trying to boot. Once you have a
U-Boot shell, enter in the following network settings:

```console
setenv ipaddr <versal_ip>
setenv netmask <netmask>
setenv serverip <nfs_server_ip>
ping <nfs_server_ip> # OPTIONAL: Make sure you can ping host
setenv bootcmd 'if pxe get; then pxe boot; fi'

```
Where:
- `<versal_ip>`: IP address of the Versal
- `<netmask>`: Your netmask IP configuration (e.g. `255.255.255.0`)
- `<nfs_server_ip>`: IP address of host NFS server

The above network settings should match the network settings within your
customized [pxeboot configuration
file](helper_scripts/pxelinux.cfg/default-arm-versal).

## Branches

There are 3 seperate branches for the design:
- [main](https://github.com/nasa-jpl/versal-sar-backprojection-design/tree/main)
- [host_stride](https://github.com/nasa-jpl/versal-sar-backprojection-design/tree/host_stride)
- [pl_stride](https://github.com/nasa-jpl/versal-sar-backprojection-design/tree/pl_stride)

The features of these branches are further discussed in
[doc/versal_sar_backproject.pdf](doc/versal_sar_backproject.pdf).

## Documentation Generation

The following packages were installed for documentation generation:
- `latexmk` - Automates compiling LaTeX documents
- `zathura` - Document viewer
- `zathura-pdf-poppler` - Plugin to add PDF support for Zathura
- `texlive-latex-extra` - Adds .svg image support
- `inkscape` - Graphics support

## FAQ

1. Why doesn't this repo contain everything necessary to build this design?

In order to promote better version control practices, dependency management,
and extensibility, different elements of building out designs for the Versal
ACAP are stored in their own repositories. For example, All the repos necessary
for building the Linux OS running on the ARM of the Versal are pulled out into
their own repository (see the
[versal-manifest](https://github.com/nasa-jpl/versal-manifest) repo to see

# By: Austin Owens
# Date: 5/21/2024
# Desc: Makefile for building various elements of the design
#
# Targets: package, run, pl, plsim_router, aie, host, aiesim, aiesim_profile, aiesim_xpe, metrics, clean
# 
# Examples:
# make
# make aie
# make aiesim
# make host
# make package
# make TARGET=sw_emu run
# make TARGET=hw_emu run


##### VARIABLES #####

# User Defined Variables
TARGET ?= hw

# Global Vars
XSA = sar_backproject_${TARGET}.xsa
HOST_EXE = sar_backproject.elf
PROJECT_DIR = $(patsubst %/,%, $(dir $(realpath $(firstword $(MAKEFILE_LIST)))))
EMU_LAUNCH_FILE = launch_${TARGET}.sh
ifeq ($(TARGET), sw_emu)
    AIE_TARGET = x86sim
    PL_TARGET = x86
else
    AIE_TARGET = hw
    PL_TARGET = hw
endif

# Build Directories
BUILD_DIR = build/${TARGET}
AIE_BUILD_DIR = ${BUILD_DIR}/aie/${AIE_TARGET}
PL_BUILD_DIR = ${BUILD_DIR}/pl/${TARGET}
AIESIM_BUILD_DIR = ${BUILD_DIR}/aiesim
PLSIM_BUILD_DIR = ${BUILD_DIR}/plsim
HOST_BUILD_DIR = ${BUILD_DIR}/host
XSA_BUILD_DIR = ${BUILD_DIR}/xsa
PACKAGE_BUILD_DIR = ${BUILD_DIR}/package
METRICS_BUILD_DIR = build/hw/metrics

##### CHECKS #####

# Check valid TARGET value
VALID_TARGETS := hw hw_emu sw_emu
ifeq ($(filter $(TARGET),$(VALID_TARGETS)),)
    $(error Invalid TARGET specified: $(TARGET). Valid options are 'hw', 'hw_emu', or 'sw_emu')
endif

# Check if PLATFORM is set from the environment
ifndef PLATFORM
    $(error PLATFORM is not set. Please source the env_setup.sh script.)
endif

# Check for incompatible TARGET=sw_emu and 'aiesim' combination
ifneq (,$(filter aiesim,$(MAKECMDGOALS)))
ifeq ($(TARGET), sw_emu)
    $(error The 'aiesim' target cannot be used with 'sw_emu'. \
The AI Engine simulator (aiesimulator) models the timing and resources of \
the AI Engine array and requires the application to be compiled with \
hardware (hw) or hardware emulation (hw_emu) targets to provide \
cycle-accurate performance analysis. The 'sw_emu' target uses the x86 \
simulator, which provides a fast functional simulation without timing \
accuracy. Please use 'hw' or 'hw_emu' for accurate AI Engine simulation)
endif
endif

# Check for incompatible TARGET=hw and 'run' combination
ifneq (,$(filter run,$(MAKECMDGOALS)))
ifeq ($(TARGET), hw)
    $(error The 'run' target can only be used with a TARGET=hw_emu or TARGET=sw_emu)
endif
endif

.PHONY: package run pl plsim_router aie aiesim aiesim_profile host aiesim_xpe metrics clean


##### DIRECT TARGETS #####

# Packaging target for linking everything together (only package the DTB with hw since
# custom DTB's seems to cause the kernel to panic and crash when QEMU is used)
ifeq ($(TARGET),hw)
    DTB_OPTION := --package.dtb ${DTB}
else
    DTB_OPTION :=
endif
package: ${PL_BUILD_DIR}/dma_pkt_router.xo ${AIE_BUILD_DIR}/libadf.a ${HOST_BUILD_DIR}/${HOST_EXE} ${XSA_BUILD_DIR}/${XSA} 
	@RC_SAMPLES=$$(grep '^#define RC_SAMPLES' ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/common.h | awk '{print $$3}'); \
	mkdir -p ${PACKAGE_BUILD_DIR}; \
	cd ${PACKAGE_BUILD_DIR}; \
	v++ -p -t ${TARGET} -f ${PLATFORM} \
		$(DTB_OPTION) \
		--package.bl31_elf ${BL31_ELF} \
		--package.uboot ${UBOOT} \
		--package.kernel_image ${IMAGE} \
		--package.rootfs ${ROOTFS} \
		--package.boot_mode=sd \
		--package.image_format=ext4 \
		--package.defer_aie_run \
		--package.sd_file ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/exec_scripts/run_script_${TARGET}.sh \
		--package.sd_file ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/profiling_cfgs/xrt.ini \
		--package.sd_file ${PROJECT_DIR}/${HOST_BUILD_DIR}/${HOST_EXE} \
		--package.sd_file ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/test_data/gotcha_slowtime_pass1_360deg_HH.csv \
		--package.sd_file ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/test_data/gotcha_phdata_$${RC_SAMPLES}-out-of-424-rc-samples_pass1_360deg_HH.csv \
		${PROJECT_DIR}/${XSA_BUILD_DIR}/${XSA} ${PROJECT_DIR}/${AIE_BUILD_DIR}/libadf.a

	@echo "Packaging Complete..."
	@echo "####################################"
	@echo ""

# Run target for running emulation. Influenced by TARGET being sw_emu or hw_emu.
run: package
	${PACKAGE_BUILD_DIR}/${EMU_LAUNCH_FILE}
	@echo ""
	@echo "Emulation Finished..."
	@echo "####################################"
	@echo ""

# PL target for building all HLS Programmable Logic (PL) kernels
pl: ${PL_BUILD_DIR}/dma_pkt_router.xo

# PL sim target for building all artifacts needed for running the packet router
# PL sim. If the CSV file doesn't exist, run aiesim to generate it.
plsim_router:
	if [ ! -f ${AIESIM_BUILD_DIR}/aiesimulator_output/aie_to_plio_switch_0_0.csv ]; then \
	    $(MAKE) aiesim; \
	fi
	mkdir -p ${PLSIM_BUILD_DIR}/plsimulator_output; \
	cd ${PLSIM_BUILD_DIR}; \
	vitis-run --tcl ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/pl/tb/run_dma_pkt_router_tb.tcl | tee plsim_router.log
	@echo ""
	@echo "DMA Packet Router PL Simulation, Complete..."
	@echo "####################################"
	@echo ""


# AIE target for building all AIE related apps
aie: ${AIE_BUILD_DIR}/libadf.a

# Host target for building all host related apps
host: ${HOST_BUILD_DIR}/${HOST_EXE}

# AIE simulation target
aiesim: ${AIE_BUILD_DIR}/libadf.a
	mkdir -p ${AIESIM_BUILD_DIR}; \
	cd ${AIESIM_BUILD_DIR}; \
	aiesimulator --pkg-dir=${PROJECT_DIR}/${BUILD_DIR}/Work \
		--input-dir ${PROJECT_DIR}/${PLSIM_BUILD_DIR}/plsimulator_output 2>&1 | tee aiesim.log
	@echo ""
	@echo "AIE Simulation, Without Profiling, Complete..."
	@echo "####################################"
	@echo ""

# AIE simulation target that enables profiling. This allows prints to appear in
# console in AIE kernel code and also generates profile information.
aiesim_profile: ${AIE_BUILD_DIR}/libadf.a
	mkdir -p ${AIESIM_BUILD_DIR}; \
	cd ${AIESIM_BUILD_DIR}; \
	aiesimulator --profile --pkg-dir=${PROJECT_DIR}/${BUILD_DIR}/Work \
		--dump-vcd aie \
		--input-dir ${PROJECT_DIR}/${PLSIM_BUILD_DIR}/plsimulator_output 2>&1 | tee aiesim.log
	@echo ""
	@echo "AIE Simulation, With Profiling, Complete..."
	@echo "####################################"
	@echo ""

# Generates power metrics for AIE using the aie.vcd generated by the aiesimulator. The xpe
# file can be used in addition to the xpe file generated from the 'metrics' target to 
# generate a more comprehensive power estimation. You can use the PDM GUI to import these 
# files to look at these various power-related metrics.
aiesim_xpe: ${AIE_BUILD_DIR}/libadf.a ${AIESIM_BUILD_DIR}/aie.vcd
	mkdir -p ${METRICS_BUILD_DIR}; \
	cd ${METRICS_BUILD_DIR}; \
	vcdanalyze --vcd ${PROJECT_DIR}/${AIESIM_BUILD_DIR}/aie.vcd \
		--pkg-dir=${PROJECT_DIR}/${BUILD_DIR}/Work \
		--xpe
	@echo ""
	@echo "AIE XPE Generation Complete..."
	@echo "####################################"
	@echo ""

# Generate utilization and power metrics from entire project. TARGET must be HW.
metrics: ${XSA_BUILD_DIR}/${XSA}
	mkdir -p $(METRICS_BUILD_DIR); \
	cd $(METRICS_BUILD_DIR); \
	vivado -mode batch -source ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/vivado_metrics_scripts/report_metrics.tcl \
		${PROJECT_DIR}/$(XSA_BUILD_DIR)/_x/link/vivado/vpl/prj/prj.xpr
	@echo ""
	@echo "Vivado Utilization/Power Report Generation Complete..."
	@echo "####################################"
	@echo ""

##### INDIRECT TARGETS #####

# Building DMA Packet Router PL kernel
${PL_BUILD_DIR}/dma_pkt_router.xo: design/pl/dma_pkt_router.cpp design/pl/dma_pkt_router.h design/pl/pkt_router_config.cfg ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/common.h
	@AIE_SWITCHES=$$(grep '^#define AIE_SWITCHES' ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/common.h | awk '{print $$3}'); \
	echo "# THIS FILE IS AUTO-GENERATED FROM THE MAKEFILE" > ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/system_cfgs/system.cfg; \
	echo -e "\n[clock]" >> ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/system_cfgs/system.cfg; \
	echo -e "default_freqhz=312500000\n" >> ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/system_cfgs/system.cfg; \
	echo "[connectivity]" >> ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/system_cfgs/system.cfg; \
	echo -e "\n### DMA PACKET ROUTER CONTROLLER ###" >> ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/system_cfgs/system.cfg; \
    routers=$$(printf "dma_pkt_router_%s," $$(seq 0 $$((AIE_SWITCHES - 1)))); \
	routers=$${routers%,}; \
	echo "nk=dma_pkt_router:$$AIE_SWITCHES:$$routers" >> ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/system_cfgs/system.cfg; \
	echo -e "\n# Connect AIE graph's plio_pkt_rtr_out_0_# to PL kernel's pl_stream_in" >> ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/system_cfgs/system.cfg; \
	for i in $$(seq 0 $$((AIE_SWITCHES - 1))); do \

	done; \
	echo -e "\n# System port connection linking dma_pkt_router_0 instance to mem resource" >> ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/system_cfgs/system.cfg; \
	for i in $$(seq 0 $$((AIE_SWITCHES - 1))); do \
		echo "sp=dma_pkt_router_$$i.ddr_mem:DDR" >> ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/system_cfgs/system.cfg; \
	done; \
	mkdir -p ${PL_BUILD_DIR}; \
	cd ${PL_BUILD_DIR}; \
	v++ -c --mode hls --platform=${PLATFORM} -t ${PL_TARGET} \
		--work_dir=${PROJECT_DIR}/${BUILD_DIR}/Work \
		--config ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/pl/pkt_router_config.cfg; \
	mv ${PROJECT_DIR}/${BUILD_DIR}/Work/dma_pkt_router.xo ./
	@echo ""
	@echo "DMA Packet Router PL Kernel Built..."
	@echo "####################################"
	@echo ""

# Building the ADF library
${AIE_BUILD_DIR}/libadf.a: design/aie/* ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/common.h design/aie/aiecompiler.cfg
	mkdir -p ${AIE_BUILD_DIR}; \
	cd ${AIE_BUILD_DIR}; \
	v++ -c --mode aie --platform=${PLATFORM} -t ${AIE_TARGET} \
		--config ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/aie/aiecompiler.cfg \
		--work_dir=${PROJECT_DIR}/${BUILD_DIR}/Work \
		--include="${PROJECT_DIR}/design/aie" \
		--include=$(DSPLIB_VITIS)/dsp/L1/src/aie \
		--include=$(DSPLIB_VITIS)/dsp/L1/include/aie \
		--include=$(DSPLIB_VITIS)/dsp/L2/include/aie \
		${PROJECT_DIR}/design/aie/graph.cpp

# Building the host executable
${HOST_BUILD_DIR}/${HOST_EXE}: ${AIE_BUILD_DIR}/libadf.a ${BUILD_DIR}/Work/ps/c_rts/aie_control.cpp design/host/* ${PROJECT_DIR}/design/common.h

# Building the XSA

19	\gls{sar} is a radar imaging modality that enables high-resolution imagery by
20	using antenna motion over the scene and combining measurements from many nearby
21	positions along the flight path, shown in figure
22	\ref{fig:sar-flight-path-geometry-data}. At centimeter wavelengths, achieving
23	about ten meter resolution on the ground with a single antenna would require an
24	antenna several kilometers long from orbit and still tens to a few hundred
25	meters from typical aircraft, which is not realistic to build or fly. During
26	processing, the many measurements are combined so they behave as if they were
27	taken with a much longer antenna, which provides the needed resolution without
28	a very large physical antenna. Because SAR does not rely on sunlight, it can
29	image day or night and in most weather conditions, supporting Earth
30	observation, hazard assessment, sea-ice tracking, wetland mapping, and broader
31	environmental monitoring~\cite{NASAEarthdataSAR}.
32	
33	A few geometry terms appear throughout this paper. The flight direction is the
34	along-track or azimuth direction and the perpendicular direction is the
35	across-track or range direction. The distance measured along the radar line of
36	sight is the slant range, which can be projected to ground range. The look
37	angle describes how far the antenna points away from nadir, while the incidence
38	angle is the angle between the radar beam and the local surface normal.
39	Depending on terrain and viewing geometry, SAR images can contain layover and
40	shadow.
41	
42	The work throughout this paper focuses on spotlight-mode backprojection, an
43	image reconstruction technique that operates on the raw complex radar
44	measurements known as phase-history data. Stripmap-mode backprojection is left
45	for future work (see Section~\ref{sec:stripmap_mode} for more details). For
46	each image pixel, backprojection uses the recorded platform trajectory to
47	compute the two-way travel time to that pixel for every pulse. Each recorded
48	echo is aligned to that pixel by applying the computed delay. This can be done
49	by shifting the waveform in time or by applying the corresponding phase shift
50	across the signal’s bandwidth. After alignment, the echoes are summed. When the
51	delays match the true geometry and timing, the aligned echoes add in phase at
52	that pixel and tend to cancel elsewhere, producing a focused image. Because
53	backprojection coherently combines many pulses for every pixel, the echoes from
54	the true location align in phase and reinforce, increasing the pixel’s
55	intensity even when the platform does not fly a perfectly straight path or the
56	viewing geometry is not ideal, provided the trajectory and timing are modeled
57	with sufficient accuracy. These strengths come with significant computational
58	cost. Consequently, many operational systems transmit phase-history data to the
59	ground and form images there rather than on board.

79	\cite{AMD_Versal_WP505}. We design and integrate a data path from the dual

2	\section{AI Engine Overview}
3	% =============================================================================
4	\label{sec:overview}
5	
6	
7	\subsection{Parallelism and Data Transfer}
8	\label{sec:parallelism_and_data_trans}
9	
10	% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
11	% AI Engine Array
12	% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
13	\begin{figure}[hbtp]
14	  \begin{center}
15	    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]
16	    {figures/aie_array.png}
17	  \end{center}
18	  \caption{AI Engine Array \cite{AMD_Versal_AM009}}
19	  \label{fig:aie_array}
20	\end{figure}
21	% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
22	
23	AI Engines are an array of \gls{vliw} processors with \gls{simd} vector units
24	that are highly optimized for compute-intensive applications
25	\cite{AMD_Versal_UG1079}. The AI Engine array supports three levels of
26	parallelism:
27	
28	\begin{itemize}
29	    \item \textbf{\gls{ilp}:} Through the VLIW architecture allowing multiple
30	        operations to be executed in a single clock cycle.
31	    \item \textbf{SIMD:} Through vector registers allowing multiple elements
32	        to be computed in parallel.
33	    \item \textbf{Multicore:} Through the AI Engine array, allowing up to 400
34	        AI Engine tiles to execute in parallel.
35	\end{itemize}
36	
37	Additionally, the AI Engine tiles provide multiple mechanisms to store,
38	pipeline, and move data. Figure~\ref{fig:aie_array} highlights several of these
39	data-transfer mechanisms. The following list gives a more complete overview:
40	
41	\begin{itemize}
42	  \item \textbf{Local memory} - Each tile has 32\,KB of data memory for runtime
43	      buffers.
44	  \item \textbf{Neighbor memory sharing} - A tile can directly access adjacent
45	      tiles’ memories with hardware locks for coordination, effectively
46	      expanding local storage~\cite{AMD_Versal_UG1079}.
47	  \item \textbf{Cascade ports} - Dedicated links between adjacent AI Engine
48	      tiles’ \gls{mac} accumulators used to pass partial sums or intermediate
49	      results. This path bypasses AXI4-Stream and local memory for low-latency
50	      chained computations.
51	  \item \textbf{AXI4-Stream (tile-to-tile)} - General-purpose streaming
52	      interfaces inside the AI Engine array (typically 32 bits per port) with
53	      handshake signals (\textit{TVALID}, \textit{TREADY}, and often
54	      \textit{TLAST} for frame boundaries).
55	  \item \textbf{PLIO ports} - AXI4-Stream connections between the AI Engine
56	      array and the PL; commonly 32, 64, or 128 bits wide at the interface
57	      boundary.
58	  \item \textbf{GMIO ports} - Interfaces that move data between external DDR
59	      via the \gls{noc} and the AI Engine array. Support burst transfers (e.g.,
60	      64/128/256\,B).
61	  \item \textbf{Memory-mapped access (NoC)} - For control or lower-bandwidth
62	      data movement, the NoC can read/write local memories and configure DMA
63	      descriptors using AXI memory-mapped transactions.
64	\end{itemize}
65	
66	\subsection{AI Engine Kernels}
67	\label{subsec:aie_kernels}
68	
69	
70	\subsubsection{Overview}
71	\label{subsubsec:overview}
72	
73	An AI Engine kernel is a C/C++ function written with the AI Engine API that
74	targets the VLIW vector processor in each AI Engine tile. Arrays range from
75	tens to hundreds of tiles depending on the device; for example, the AI Core
76	VC1902 integrates 400 AI Engine tiles~\cite{AMD_Versal_DS946}. Kernels are
77	compiled with the Vitis AI Engine compiler into ELF images, which the graph
78	runtime loads onto the assigned tiles. Based on the user-specified runtime
79	ratio and available resources, the compiler may co-locate two kernels to

86	restructuring to expose vector and instruction-level parallelism. In practice
87	we express arithmetic with AI Engine intrinsics such as \verb|aie::add()|,
88	\verb|aie::sub()|, and \verb|aie::mul()|, while local data storage and
89	retrieval is handled explicitly with vector stores and loads (e.g.,

92	vector registers, and help the compiler generate packed stores/loads and fused
93	multiply–accumulate sequences. Without this structure, code is often scalarized
94	by the compiler, underutilizing the vector hardware.

97	\label{subsubsec:pipelining_and_data_movement}
98

101	and buffering. For example, using ping-pong (double) buffers or circular
102	buffers allows one memory block to be used for computing while the other is
103	loaded or stored, effectively overlapping memory access with computation. When
104	buffers are aligned and accessed contiguously, the compiler can issue one
105	vector multiply–accumulate per cycle (subject to memory-port bandwidth) by
106	preloading operands for the next iteration while writing results from the prior
107	one. Developers can also guide the compiler with the
108	\verb|chess_prepare_for_pipelining| directive, which prompts the AI Engine
109	compiler to create an overlapped (software-pipelined)
110	schedule~\cite{AMD_Versal_UG1079}. By contrast, \gls{hls} pipeline pragmas like
111	\texttt{\#pragma HLS PIPELINE II=1} target PL kernels and are not used for AI

114	on memory rather than keeping the AI Engine’s resources busy.

116	
117	\subsubsection{Buffer and Stream Interfaces}

124	kernel proceeds~\cite{AMD_Versal_UG1079}. If multiple synchronous input buffers
125	are declared, the kernel will not fire until all are ready. By contrast, an
126	asynchronous buffer port (declared with \texttt{async} in the buffer type name)

128	releases the buffer to control when data is accessed, giving the designer more
129	flexibility but also the responsibility for synchronization.

132	With streams, the kernel can keep reading or writing beats of data without
133	waiting for a full block. AI Engine graphs support bi-directional stream ports
134	(and dedicated cascade streams between neighbors) that run at full
135	bandwidth~\cite{AMD_Versal_UG1079}. In effect, streaming ports create an
136	endless data pipeline: as soon as data is available on the stream, the kernel
137	can process it beat-by-beat. For example, a PL-side AXI stream input can feed
138	into the AI Engine via a PLIO port, and the kernel’s code can simply advance a
139	stream iterator each cycle.

145	the \gls{adf} API. This graph defines kernels, ports, and the connections
146	between them (Figure~\ref{fig:aie_graph}). The ADF graph can interface with the

160	ping–pong buffers) so that kernels can compute on one block while the next
161	block is being filled. For stream connections, data flows continuously without
162	explicit buffering.
163	
164	Graph execution follows a Kahn process-network model where each kernel fires
165	only when its inputs are ready, making kernel execution data-driven. This
166	enables concurrency across the graph where one kernel may compute while another
167	loads the next data block and a third writes results. Together with loop-level
168	pipelining inside kernels, graph-level concurrency maximizes throughput across
169	the AI Engine array.

% =============================================================================

\subsection{Parallelism and Data Transfer}
\label{sec:parallelism_and_data_trans}

% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
% AI Engine Array
% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{figure}[hbtp]
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]
    {figures/aie_array.png}
  \end{center}
  \caption{AI Engine Array \cite{AMD_Versal_AM009}}
  \label{fig:aie_array}
\end{figure}
% -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

AI Engines are an array of \gls{vliw} processors with \gls{simd} vector units
that are highly optimized for compute-intensive applications
\cite{AMD_Versal_UG1079}. The AI Engine array supports three levels of
parallelism:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{\gls{ilp}:} Through the VLIW architecture allowing multiple
        operations to be executed in a single clock cycle.
    \item \textbf{SIMD:} Through vector registers allowing multiple elements
        to be computed in parallel.
    \item \textbf{Multicore:} Through the AI Engine array, allowing up to 400
        AI Engine tiles to execute in parallel.
\end{itemize}

Additionally, the AI Engine tiles provide multiple mechanisms to store,
pipeline, and move data. Figure~\ref{fig:aie_array} highlights several of these
data-transfer mechanisms. The following list gives a more complete overview:

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Local memory} - Each tile has 32\,KB of data memory for runtime
      buffers.
  \item \textbf{Neighbor memory sharing} - A tile can directly access adjacent
      tiles’ memories with hardware locks for coordination, effectively
      expanding local storage~\cite{AMD_Versal_UG1079}.
  \item \textbf{Cascade ports} - Dedicated links between adjacent AI Engine
      tiles’ \gls{mac} accumulators used to pass partial sums or intermediate
      results. This path bypasses AXI4-Stream and local memory for low-latency
      chained computations.
  \item \textbf{AXI4-Stream (tile-to-tile)} - General-purpose streaming
      interfaces inside the AI Engine array (typically 32 bits per port) with
      handshake signals (\textit{TVALID}, \textit{TREADY}, and often
      \textit{TLAST} for frame boundaries).
  \item \textbf{PLIO ports} - AXI4-Stream connections between the AI Engine
      array and the PL; commonly 32, 64, or 128 bits wide at the interface
      boundary.
  \item \textbf{GMIO ports} - Interfaces that move data between external DDR
      via the \gls{noc} and the AI Engine array. Support burst transfers (e.g.,
      64/128/256\,B).
  \item \textbf{Memory-mapped access (NoC)} - For control or lower-bandwidth
      data movement, the NoC can read/write local memories and configure DMA
      descriptors using AXI memory-mapped transactions.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{AI Engine Kernels}
\label{subsec:aie_kernels}


\subsubsection{Overview}
\label{subsubsec:overview}

An AI Engine kernel is a C/C++ function written with the AI Engine API that
targets the VLIW vector processor in each AI Engine tile. Arrays range from
tens to hundreds of tiles depending on the device; for example, the AI Core
VC1902 integrates 400 AI Engine tiles~\cite{AMD_Versal_DS946}. Kernels are
compiled with the Vitis AI Engine compiler into ELF images, which the graph
runtime loads onto the assigned tiles. Based on the user-specified runtime
ratio and available resources, the compiler may co-locate two kernels to
time-share a tile. If not, it assigns one kernel to the tile.

\label{subsubsec:simd}

\label{subsubsec:pipelining_and_data_movement}

\subsubsection{Buffer and Stream Interfaces}
\label{subsubsec:buffer_and_stream_inf}

ports. A buffer port maps to a contiguous block of local tile memory that

are declared, the kernel will not fire until all are ready. By contrast, an

\label{subsec:aie_graphs}

between them (Figure~\ref{fig:aie_graph}). The ADF graph can interface with the
PL, global memory, and the host processor using specialized ports, such as:

\begin{itemize}
\item \texttt{input\_plio} and \texttt{output\_plio}: AXI-stream connections to
    and from the PL.
\item \texttt{input\_gmio} and \texttt{output\_gmio}: memory-mapped DMA
    connections to and from global memory (e.g., DDR).
\item \gls{rtp}: passes runtime parameter data to AI Engine kernels (primarily
    for passing single values or small arrays).
\end{itemize}

At runtime, the Vitis toolchain manages data movement across these connections.
For buffer connections, it automatically implements double-buffering (e.g.,
ping–pong buffers) so that kernels can compute on one block while the next
block is being filled. For stream connections, data flows continuously without
explicit buffering.

Graph execution follows a Kahn process-network model where each kernel fires
only when its inputs are ready, making kernel execution data-driven. This
enables concurrency across the graph where one kernel may compute while another
loads the next data block and a third writes results. Together with loop-level
pipelining inside kernels, graph-level concurrency maximizes throughput across
the AI Engine array.

\label{subsec:quick_ref}

\begin{itemize}[parsep=1em]
    \item GMIO Ports (DDR $\leftrightarrow$ NoC $\leftrightarrow$ AI Engine)
        \begin{itemize}[topsep=0em]
            \item 32 GMIO input ports at the graph/system level
            \item 32 GMIO output ports at the graph/system level
            \item Common NoC burst sizes: 64B, 128B, or 256B.
        \end{itemize}

    \item PLIO Ports ($PL \leftrightarrow AI Engine$)
        \begin{itemize}[topsep=0em]
            \item Configurable bus widths: 32b, 64b, or 128b.
            \item 32 bits per AI Engine clock (i.e. each 32b take 1 clk cycle

        \end{itemize}

    \item Clocks

            \item NoC clock: approximately 1.0 GHz.
            \item PL clocks: approximately 500 MHz (but can vary widely).
            \item ARM Cortex-A72: approximately 1.35 GHz (also

        \end{itemize}

        \begin{itemize}[topsep=0em]
            \item 32 KB total per tile for runtime data:

        \begin{itemize}[topsep=0em]
            \item 16 KB for application program memory size (separate from the

        \end{itemize}

    \item AI Engine AXI4 Stream I/O
        \begin{itemize}[topsep=0em]
            \item Up to 2 input and 2 output streaming ports, each 32 bits

            \item Internal FIFOs enable packing 128 bits every 4 cycles,

1	% =============================================================================
2	\section{Implementation}
3	% =============================================================================
4	\label{sec:impl}
5	
6	% =============================================================================
7	\subsection{Algorithmic Basis and Dataset}
8	% =============================================================================
9	
10	This design builds upon the mathematical formulations presented in the "SAR
11	Image Formation Toolbox for MATLAB" by Gorham et al.~\cite{Gorham}. The toolbox
12	implements a backprojection algorithm in spotlight mode using the "Gotcha
13	Volumetric SAR Data Set, Version 1.0" as its primary example~\cite{GOTCHA}.
14	This dataset, collected at X-band with a 640~MHz bandwidth, includes full
15	azimuth coverage across eight elevation angles and complete polarization. The
16	imaging scene contains civilian vehicles and calibration targets, making it a
17	standard benchmark for validating SAR image-formation methods.
18	
19	The dataset is distributed in MATLAB binary format (*.mat). Each file
20	represents one degree of azimuth for a single pass and polarization, and
21	contains phase-history samples, frequency vectors, antenna coordinates (X, Y,
22	Z), range to scene center, and azimuth/elevation angles. These measurements
23	supply both the raw radar returns and the platform geometry needed to drive the
24	backprojection reconstruction.
25	
26	In this work, Gorham’s mathematical formulation and dataset are mapped onto
27	Versal hardware to evaluate parallelization strategies. Focused images produced
28	by the AI Engine implementation are compared against the MATLAB reference
29	outputs. Appendix \ref{sec:matlab_appendix} contains more information on how the
30	MATLAB code was used and how the dataset was used to generate the input data
31	for the AI Engine.
32	
33	The following sections describe how this algorithm and dataset are mapped onto
34	the Versal ACAP architecture, including the division of responsibilities across
35	the AI Engine, programmable logic, and ARM cores.
36	
37	% =============================================================================
38	\subsection{Algorithm Mapping to Hardware}
39	% =============================================================================
40	
41	The Versal architecture was used to accelerate the Gorham backprojection
42	formulation. Typical acceleration methods on the Versal are expressed through
43	SIMD intrinsics, multi-core instantiation, and ILP. The current implementation
44	heavily emphasizes SIMD and multi-core parallelism. While some ILP
45	optimizations were implemented, further ILP modifications could potentially be
46	made and are reserved for future work (see
47	Section~\ref{sec:ilp_optimizations}). Accuracy is validated by comparing
48	focused images from the Versal hardware and AI Engine simulations against
49	MATLAB reference outputs.
50	
51	During development, multiple custom AI Engine and PL kernel designs were
52	evaluated. The finalized design includes three types of AI Engine kernels and
53	up to two PL kernels (depending on the build branch described in
54	Section~\ref{sec:system_overview}). These kernels can be instantiated a
55	specific number of times based on the build configuration. The summary of
56	these kernels, along with how many times the they can be instantiated in the
57	current design, are listed below:
58	
59	\subsubsection{AI Engine Kernels}
60	\begin{itemize}
61	    \item \textbf{Data Broadcast Kernel (1x):} Distributes slow-time radar data
62	        (antenna coordinates, range-to-scene center) and range-compressed
63	        samples to all Image Reconstruction kernels.
64	    \item \textbf{Pixel Demux Kernel (1x-7x):} Assigns target pixels of
65	        interest to the Image Reconstruction kernels. In the \textit{main}
66	        branch, this kernel also performs input sorting. In
67	        \textit{host\_stride} and \textit{pl\_stride}, sorting is performed by
68	        the ARM or PL, respectively.
69	    \item \textbf{Image Reconstruction Kernel (1x-224x):} Implements the core 
70	        backprojection loop. For each pixel, it computes the differential 
71	        range relative to the scene center, applies phase correction, and 
72	        accumulates contributions across pulses. These kernels exploit SIMD 
73	        vectorization to maximize throughput.
74	\end{itemize}
75	
76	\subsubsection{PL Kernels}
77	\begin{itemize}
78	    \item \textbf{DMA Packet Router Kernel (1x-7x):} Reorders merged
79	        AXI4-Stream outputs from the AI Engine into contiguous memory in DDR,
80	        ensuring that image pixels are correctly placed for reconstruction.
81	    \item \textbf{DMA Stride Controller Kernel (1x-7x):} Reads and reorders
82	        specific data segments from DDR before streaming them into the AI
83	        Engine, offloading the input-sorting responsibility from the ARM or AI
84	        Engine.
85	\end{itemize}
86	
87	These kernels form the building blocks of the overall processing chain. A
88	scaled-down version of the design showing how these kernels interconnect are
89	displayed in Figure~\ref{fig:aie_graph}. The next section presents the
90	system-level overview and how data flows and interacts through the system as a
91	whole.
92	
93	% =============================================================================
94	\subsection{System Overview}
95	% =============================================================================
96	\label{sec:system_overview}
97	
98	The design integrates the ARM Cortex-A72 processor, the AI Engine array, and
99	the PL. At a high-level, the ARM Cortex-A72 is responsible for the following
100	tasks:
101	
102	\begin{itemize}
103	    \item Retrieves input data from non-volatile memory and orchestrates
104	        dataflow throughout the system.
105	    \item Manages PL kernel and AI Engine graph control execution.
106	    \item Configures kernel parameters.
107	    \item Records performance metrics.
108	\end{itemize}
109	
110	\noindent The AI Engine array is responsible for the following tasks:
111	
112	\begin{itemize}
113	    \item Parallelizes the backprojection algorithm across several AI kernels.
114	    \item Vectorizes the backprojection algorithm on each AI kernel.
115	    \item Performs minimal ILP through for loop pipelining.
116	    \item Sorts pixels into specific AI kernels (based on which branch of the
117	        code is being ran).
118	    \item Focuses image data per pulse until the ARM processor signals an RTP
119	        signal.
120	\end{itemize}
121	
122	\noindent The PL acts as a custom DMA controller and is responsible for the
123	following tasks:
124	
125	\begin{itemize}
126	    \item Post-processing the data after AI Engine egress by reordering packets
127	        into DDR.
128	    \item Pre-processing the data before AI Engine ingress by reordering
129	        packets from DDR (based on which branch of the code is being ran).
130	\end{itemize}
131	
132	\noindent There are three branch configurations to compare performance
133	trade-offs:
134	
135	\begin{itemize}
136	    \item \textbf{main:} The AI Engine kernels ingest unsorted data and perform 
137	        their own input reordering before computation.
138	    \item \textbf{host\_stride:} The ARM Cortex-A72 pre-sorts the data in DDR, 
139	        reducing the sorting work inside the AI Engine.
140	    \item \textbf{pl\_stride:} The PL handles the pre-processing by implementing
141	        a DMA stride controller that pre-sorts the data before it reaches the
142	        AI Engine.
143	\end{itemize}
144	
145	Regardless if pre-processing is handled in the AI Engine, ARM, or PL, the
146	post-processing is always handled within the PL logic. This is required because
147	packet stream mergers are used inside the AI Engine to collapse many kernel
148	outputs into the limited set of GMIO ports (32 input and 32 output). While
149	merging improves GMIO port utilization, it scrambles output order. A PL packet
150	router therefore inspects packet IDs on the AXI streams and reorders them into
151	a contiguous layout in DDR, so the final image is coherent without additional
152	post-processing work by the ARM processor.

278	\subsubsection{Data Broadcast Kernel}
279	% =============================================================================
280	\label{subsec:data_broadcasting_kern}
281	
282	There is only one Data Broadcast kernel that needs to be instantiated in the
283	design. The Data Broadcast kernel receives its data from the ARM processor via
284	DDR through two GMIO ports (slowtime\_in and rc\_in) and it broadcasts its data
285	via two output ports (slowtime\_out and rc\_out) feeding into the Image
286	Reconstruction kernel. The slowtime\_in and slowtime\_out ports transfer
287	AXI4-Stream data and rc\_in and rc\_out ports transfer buffered ping-pong data.
288	The inputs and outputs for the Data Broadcast kernel are listed below:
289	
290	\begin{itemize}
291	    \item \textbf{slowtime\_in (float):} AXI4-Stream from the DDR
292	        originating from the ARM processor that contains antenna X, Y, Z and
293	        range to scene center.
294	    \item \textbf{rc\_in (\texttt{RC\_SAMPLES} cfloats):} Buffered range
295	        compressed phase data from the DDR originating from the ARM processor.
296	    \item \textbf{slowtime\_out (float):} AXI4-Stream that contains antenna
297	        X, Y, Z and range to scene center. This stream is broadcasted to every
298	        instantiated Image Reconstruction kernel.
299	    \item \textbf{rc\_out (\texttt{RC\_SAMPLES} cfloats):} Buffered range
300	        compressed phase data that is broadcasted to every instantiated Image
301	        Reconstruction kernel.
302	\end{itemize}
303	
304	As mentioned in Section \ref{subsec:aie_graphs}, execution of kernels begin
305	when they receive their specified number of data samples matching their
306	allocated buffer size (assuming the kernel uses any buffer types as input). The
307	Broadcast kernel only has one buffer input, which is \texttt{rc\_in} (shown in
308	Figure~\ref{fig:aie_graph}). The \texttt{rc\_in} buffer holds up to
309	\texttt{RC\_SAMPLES} cfloats, where each cfloat is 8 bytes in total (2 floats
310	for the real and imaginary numbers). Once \texttt{rc\_in} buffer is completely
311	filled, the kernel will execute. Currently, \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES} can only be
312	64, 128, 256, or 512 cfloats. 512 cfloats is the maximum size due to buffer
313	size limitations within the AI Engine. Once the Data Broadcast kernel executes,
314	it performs the following steps:
315	
316	\begin{enumerate}
317	    \item Perform a SIMD vector operation that pops 4 floats from the
318	        \texttt{slowtime\_in} AXI4-Stream port and pushes it onto the
319	        \texttt{slowtime\_out} AXI4-Stream port. This may seem redundant, but
320	        it is needed to exploit the broadcasting mechanisms within the AI
321	        Engine to broadcast the \texttt{slowtime\_out} AXI4-Stream data to all
322	        of the Image Reconstruction kernels.
323	    \item For a total of \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES}/16, perform a SIMD vector
324	        operation that pops 16 cfloats at a time from the \texttt{rc\_in}
325	        ping-pong buffer port and push them onto the \texttt{rc\_out} ping-pong
326	        buffer port.
327	    \item Once the \texttt{rc\_out} ping-pong buffer has a total of
328	        \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES} cfloats, the Broadcast kernel now has a full
329	        \texttt{rc\_out} buffer so it will automatically release lock on the
330	        \texttt{rc\_out} buffer port and forward that data out from the
331	        Broadcast kernel's local memory to all Image Reconstruction kernel
332	        memories via an AXI4-Stream burst.
333	\end{enumerate}

469	\subsubsection{Image Reconstruction Kernel}
470	% =============================================================================
471	\label{subsec:img_recon_kern}
472	
473	Image Reconstruction kernels have 4 inputs and 1 output. They receive their
474	data from multiple sources, where two of those inputs are buffered, one of the
475	inputs is an AXI4-Stream packet, and one of the inputs is an RTP value from the
476	ARM processor. The output of the kernel is the focused image and is sent as an
477	AXI4-Stream packet to an AXI4-Stream merger switch implemented on the AI
478	Engine. See Figure~\ref{fig:aie_graph} or
479	Figure~\ref{fig:aie_graph_w_stride_ctl} for a visual representation of data
480	flow connections. The inputs and outputs for the Image Reconstruction kernel
481	are listed below:
482	
483	\begin{itemize}
484	    \item \textbf{slowtime\_in (4 floats):} Buffered slowtime data containing
485	        the antenna X, Y, Z and range to target scene center.
486	    \item \textbf{rc\_in (\texttt{RC\_SAMPLES} cfloats):} Buffered range
487	        compressed phase data.
488	    \item \textbf{px\_xyz\_in (float):} AXI4-Stream packets of X, Y, and Z
489	        pixels of interest for the target scene. 
490	    \item \textbf{rtp\_dump\_img\_in (int):} RTP from ARM processor. If set to
491	        0, the kernel will continue cumulative sum operations for its current
492	        execution. If set to 1, the kernel will push the cumulative sum to the
493	        AXI4-Stream packet merger which then feeds into the DMA packet router
494	        in the PL to sort the packets into specific locations in DDR.
495	    \item \textbf{img\_out (cfloat):} AXI4-Stream packets of the phase
496	        corrected cumulative sum of a partial segment of the total target scene
497	        of interest.
498	\end{itemize}
499	
500	As mentioned in Section \ref{subsec:aie_graphs}, execution of kernels begin
501	when they receive their specified data samples matching their allocated input
502	buffer size. Additionally, if an AI kernel uses synchronous RTP's for input,
503	then the RTP port must have data sent to it first in order to meet the
504	conditions for executing the kernel. For the Image Reconstruction kernel, this
505	means the following condition must be met for it to execute once:
506	
507	\begin{itemize}
508	    \item \texttt{slowtime\_in} buffer contains 4 floats from the Data
509	        Broadcast kernel
510	    \item \texttt{rc\_in} buffer contains \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES} cfloats from the
511	        Data Broadcast kernel
512	    \item \texttt{rtp\_dump\_img\_in} RTP is passed in from the ARM processor
513	\end{itemize}
514	
515	\noindent Once the Image Reconstruction kernel executes, it performs the
516	following steps within the \textit{main} branch:
517	
518	\begin{enumerate}
519	    \item \label{itm:stream_read} Remove the AXI4-Stream header and fetch all
520	        target pixels destined for the specific Image Reconstruction kernel
521	        through the \texttt{px\_xyz\_in} AXI4-Stream packet port. The number of
522	        target pixels is based on the equation \( \frac{\texttt{PULSES} \times
523	        \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES}}{\texttt{IMG\_SOLVERS}}\). Each element from the
524	        AXI4-Stream port is of type \texttt{int} and contains the X, Y, and Z
525	        target pixel. A \texttt{reinterpret\_cast} is performed on the X, Y,
526	        and Z data to cast them into floats (since all AXI4-Stream packet data
527	        are int types by default) and place the X, Y, and Z floats into their
528	        own buffers on the heap of the running AI tile. It is important to read
529	        the \texttt{px\_xyz\_in} AXI4-Stream packet port as quickly as possible
530	        since the Pixel Demux kernel wont continue distributing target pixels
531	        to the other Image Reconstruction kernels in the \texttt{bpCluster}
532	        until it has fed all the target pixels into the Image Reconstruction
533	        kernel that it needs.
534	    \item \label{itm:buffer_load} Load 16 elements of X, Y, and Z into their
535	        own vector registers from the target pixel buffers created in step
536	        \ref{itm:stream_read}.
537	    \item \label{itm:diff_range} Calculate the differential range from the
538	        target scene center from the X, Y, and Z vector registers loaded from
539	        step \ref{itm:buffer_load}. Processing occurs at 16 pixels per clock
540	        cycle.
541	    \item \label{itm:diff_range_idx} Divide the differential range vector from
542	        step \ref{itm:diff_range} by the range resolution to get an index
543	        vector that can later be used for fetching values from \texttt{rc\_in}
544	        (used in step \ref{itm:interp}). This index vector is shifted by adding
545	        half of \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES}; this is done to properly align with the
546	        values within the \texttt{rc\_in} buffer.
547	    \item \label{itm:ph_corr} Calculate the phase correction vector for the
548	        image by multiplying the differential range vector from step
549	        \ref{itm:diff_range} by the phase correction coefficient. NOTE: Because
550	        the AI Engine API \texttt{sincos\_complex} function only works if the
551	        domain is between $-\pi$ and $\pi$, the phase correction vector from
552	        step \ref{itm:ph_corr} must be scaled up/down by $2\pi$ accordingly to
553	        fall within $-\pi$ and $\pi$. If the domain of \texttt{sincos\_complex}
554	        is not between $-\pi$ and $\pi$, the output of the function will be
555	        saturated to -1 or 1 depending on if the input value is below $-\pi$ or
556	        above $\pi$ respectively.
557	    \item \label{itm:interp} Because step \ref{itm:diff_range_idx} results in
558	        an index vector with fractional numbers, both the closest lower and
559	        upper whole number indices are derived. These integer indices are used
560	        to fetch two values from the range compressed buffer (\texttt{rc\_in})
561	        in order to perform linear interpolation in order to provide a more
562	        accurate representation of the signal at the desired fractional index.
563	        NOTE: Indexing into the \texttt{rc\_in} buffer is done \textbf{one at a
564	        time} instead of using SIMD vector operations. The algorithm breaks
565	        convention of using SIMD vector operations since the AI Engine API only
566	        support single value indexing into buffers at the time of writing; this
567	        results in a large performance hit to the algorithm. Performance
568	        improvements like this are reserved for future work. See
569	        Section~\ref{sec:aie_algo_optimization} for more details.
570	    \item \label{itm:px} Take the single interpolated range compressed value
571	        from step \ref{itm:interp} and multiply it by the phase corrected value
572	        from step \ref{itm:ph_corr} to get the phase corrected pixel in the
573	        image.
574	    \item \label{itm:img} Cumulatively add the pixel from step \ref{itm:px}
575	        into an image buffer stored in the heap of the AI Engine tile. This
576	        Image buffer persists across multiple invocations of the kernel. 
577	    \item \label{itm:inner_loop} Repeat steps \ref{itm:interp} through
578	        \ref{itm:img} for a total of 16 times to loop through all of the
579	        indices within the index vector from step \ref{itm:diff_range_idx}.
580	        NOTE: See note in step \ref{itm:interp} for why this loop is needed.
581	    \item \label{itm:main_loop} Repeat steps \ref{itm:buffer_load} through \ref{itm:inner_loop} for a
582	        total of \( \frac{\texttt{PULSES} \times
583	        \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES}}{\texttt{IMG\_SOLVERS}}\) times for all of the X,
584	        Y, and Z pixels of interest within the \texttt{px\_xy\_in} buffer.
585	    \item A single invocation of the Image Reconstruction kernel is completed.
586	        However, the \texttt{img\_out} buffer (intended for transferring the
587	        final focused image to the ARM processor) remains unwritten at this
588	        point. This is because the kernel must be invoked \texttt{PULSES} times
589	        to fully focus the image across all pulses. In each invocation, the
590	        Data Broadcast kernel provides updated slowtime data and range
591	        compressed samples. See \ref{subsec:data_broadcasting_kern} for more
592	        information on the Data Broadcast kernel. During the final pulse, the
593	        ARM processor signals the Image Reconstruction kernel to write the
594	        accumulated focused image to the \texttt{img\_out} buffer for the last
595	        invocation by setting the \texttt{rtp\_dump\_img\_in} RTP value to 1.
596	\end{enumerate}
597	
598	The \textit{host\_stride} and \textit{pl\_stride} branches have similar steps
599	as above. The only difference is step \ref{itm:stream_read} is no longer
600	performed and step \ref{itm:buffer_load} reads the target pixels directly from
601	the AXI4-Stream \texttt{px\_xyz\_in} port in 16 pixel increments. The loop in
602	step \ref{itm:main_loop} encompasses the above step so that 16 pixels will be
603	fetched from the \texttt{px\_xyz\_in} stream every iteration. This allows the
604	Pixel Demuxer kernel to Round-Robin 16 pixels at a time to each Image
605	Reconstruction kernel, then loop back to the first Image Reconstruction kernel
606	to repeat the round-robin until all pixels that are fed into the Pixel Demuxer
607	kernel are dispersed.
608	
609	% =============================================================================
610	\subsubsection{PL DMA Packet Router Kernel}
611	% =============================================================================
612	\label{subsec:pl_pkt_router_kern}
613	
614	The DMA Packet Router PL kernel is written in HLS, which allows
615	the developer to write C/C++ and compile the code into
616	synthesizable code for the FPGA. After the Image Reconstruction
617	kernels have been executed \texttt{PULSES} times and they send
618	out their focused segments of the image through \texttt{img\_out}
619	AXI4-Stream packets, a PL DMA Packet Router kernel will receive
620	the stream from each Image Reconstruction kernel within a
621	\texttt{bpCluster} and stitch them together in an ordered way
622	before placing them in DDR. This will allow the ARM processor to
623	read from DDR contiguously to see the total focused image from
624	each Image Reconstruction kernel contribution. See
625	Figure~\ref{fig:aie_graph} for a graph depicting the dataflow
626	using the DMA Packet Router PL kernel.
627	
628	\noindent The inputs and outputs for the DMA Packet Router PL kernel are listed
629	below:
630	
631	\begin{itemize}
632	    \item \textbf{pl\_stream\_in:} AXI4-Stream packets of the phase corrected
633	        cumulative sum of a partial segment of the total target scene of
634	        interest.
635	    \item \textbf{ddr\_mem:} Pointer to the 64bit DDR memory address space.
636	\end{itemize}
637	
638	\noindent The DMA Packet Router PL kernel performs the following steps:
639	
640	\begin{enumerate}
641	    \item \label{itm:pl_rtr_outer_loop} Read in first 128 bits of the
642	        AXI4-Stream packet, which will contain the packet header metadata.
643	        NOTE: The first 32 bits of this packet header contains the packet id,
644	        packet type, AI Engine tile source row, AI Engine tile source column,
645	        and the odd parity of bits 0-30. See \cite{AMD_Versal_UG1079} for more
646	        information on this packet header. The next 32 bits is the instance ID
647	        of the kernel that generated the AXI4-Stream packet. Bits 64-128 are
648	        padding and ignored. In the future, this could be used for additional
649	        metadata.
650	    \item \label{itm:pl_rtr_ddr_offset} Calculate the DDR offset location for
651	        placing the AXI4-Stream packet by taking the instance ID from the
652	        header, and multiplying it by the number of samples (\(
653	        \frac{\texttt{PULSES} \times
654	        \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES}}{\texttt{IMG\_SOLVERS}}\)) given to each Image
655	        Reconstruction kernel.
656	    \item \label{itm:pl_rtr_inner_loop} Read another 128 bits of the
657	        AXI4-Stream packet and place that image data at the specified offset
658	        derived in step \ref{itm:pl_rtr_ddr_offset}.
659	    \item \label{itm:pl_rtr_repeat} Repeat step \ref{itm:pl_rtr_inner_loop} for
660	        \( \frac{\texttt{PULSES} \times
661	        \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES}}{\texttt{IMG\_SOLVERS}}\) times
662	    \item Repeat steps \ref{itm:pl_rtr_outer_loop} through
663	        \ref{itm:pl_rtr_repeat} for \texttt{IMG\_SOLVERS\_PER\_SWITCH} times
664	\end{enumerate}
665	
666	In order for this PL kernel to be integrated into the Vivado design and a
667	complete XSA file be generated, the Vitis toolchain requires a system.cfg file
668	that specifies how the PL kernel is connected to the rest of the system. Prior
669	to the PL kernel being built, the Makefile will automatically update this
670	\textit{design/system\_cfg/system.cfg} file based on how the design is
671	configured within the \textit{design/common.h}.
672	
673	% =============================================================================
674	\subsubsection{PL DMA Stride Controller Kernel}
675	% =============================================================================
676	\label{subsec:pl_stride_kern}
677	
678	Similar to the DMA Packet Router PL kernel, the DMA Stride Controller PL kernel
679	is written in HLS. This PL kernel is only utilized within the
680	\textit{pl\_stride} branch and is only used for feeding the Pixel Demux kernel
681	with pre-sorted target pixel data from DDR. This has the following
682	implications:
683	
684	\begin{enumerate}
685	    \item The Pixel Demux kernel Round-Robins 16 target pixels at a time to
686	        each Image Reconstruction kernel within the \texttt{bpCluster} until
687	        there are no more target pixels. This is as opposed to dumping the
688	        entire set of pixels destined for a specific Image Reconstruction
689	        kernel all at once.
690	    \item The Image Reconstruction kernels can start work as soon as receiving
691	        16 target pixels as opposed to waiting for all target pixels to be
692	        collected.
693	    \item More Image Reconstruction kernels can begin working in parallel
694	        sooner since the Image Reconstruction kernels do not need to wait for
695	        the Pixel Demux kernel to fully feed the prior Image Reconstruction
696	        kernel with all its required target pixels at one time.
697	\end{enumerate}
698	
699	\noindent The inputs and outputs for the DMA Stride Controller PL kernel are
700	listed below:
701	
702	\begin{itemize}
703	    \item \textbf{ddr\_mem:} Pointer to the 64bit DDR memory address space.
704	    \item \textbf{pl\_stream\_out:} AXI4-Stream of the target pixels extracted
705	        from DDR memory. This AXI4-Stream feeds into the Pixel Demux kernel.
706	\end{itemize}
707	
708	\noindent The role of the DMA Stride Controller PL kernel performs the following steps:
709	
710	\begin{enumerate}
711	    \item \label{itm:pl_stride_inner} From the target pixel array initially
712	        passed in via the ARM processor, read in the target pixel designated at
713	        the specified target pixel array DDR memory pointer (which is index 0
714	        of the array pointer on the first iteration) and write that to the
715	        \texttt{pl\_stream\_out} AXI4-Stream. NOTE: 128 bits are read since DDR
716	        operates on 64 bit boundaries. This means that the first 64 bits
717	        contain the X and Y component of the target pixel, and the second 64
718	        bits contains the Z and a zero pad value.
719	    \item Repeat step \ref{itm:pl_stride_inner} a total of 16 times to send 16
720	        target pixels through \texttt{pl\_stream\_out} AXI4-Stream.
721	    \item \label{itm:pl_stride_middle} Shift the target pixel array DDR memory
722	        pointer by the number of target pixels destined for each AIE kernel per
723	        pulse. This equates to shifting the target pixel pointer by
724	        \(\frac{\texttt{TOTAL\_TARGET\_PIXELS}}{\texttt{IMG\_SOLVERS}}\)
725	        where: \texttt{TOTAL\_TARGET\_PIXELS} = \(\texttt{AZ\_SAMPLES} \times
726	        \texttt{RC\_SAMPLES}\).
727	    \item Repeat steps \ref{itm:pl_stride_inner} through
728	        \ref{itm:pl_stride_middle} for total of
729	        \texttt{IMG\_SOLVERS\_PER\_SWITCH} times, which is the number of Image
730	        Reconstruction kernels that are connected to the AXI4-Stream packet
731	        splitter switch. This is also the number of Image Reconstruction
732	        kernels per \texttt{bpCluster}.
733	    \item \label{itm:pl_stride_outer} At this step, the target pixel array DDR
734	        memory pointer is at the end of the target pixel array for a single
735	        \texttt{bpCluster}, so the pointer rolls back back to the beginning of
736	        the list, but offset by 16 pixels. For example, on the first iteration
737	        the base index pointer was 0, on the second iteration it would be 16,
738	        on the third it would be 32, on the fourth it would be 48, and so on.
739	    \item Repeat steps \ref{itm:pl_stride_inner} through
740	        \ref{itm:pl_stride_outer} for a total of how many multiples of 16
741	        pixels it takes to get through all the target pixels destined for a
742	        single Image Reconstruction kernel. This equates to shifting the target
743	        pixel pointer by
744	        \(\frac{\texttt{TOTAL\_TARGET\_PIXELS}}{\texttt{IMG\_SOLVERS} \times
745	        16}\).
746	    \item \label{itm:pl_stride_sw_loop} Shift the target pixel array DDR memory
747	        pointer by one whole \texttt{bpCluster}'s worth of target pixels. This would
748	        equate to shifting the target pixel pointer by
749	        \(\frac{\texttt{TOTAL\_TARGET\_PIXELS}}{\texttt{AIE\_SWITCHES}}\).
750	    \item Repeat steps \ref{itm:pl_stride_inner} through
751	        \ref{itm:pl_stride_sw_loop} for a total of \texttt{AIE\_SWITCHES} (i.e.
752	        the number of \texttt{bpCluster} units).
753	    \item \label{itm:pl_stride_pulse_loop} Shift the target pixel array DDR
754	        memory pointer by one whole pulse worth of target pixels.
755	    \item Repeat steps \ref{itm:pl_stride_inner} through
756	        \ref{itm:pl_stride_pulse_loop} for the total number of pulses
757	\end{enumerate}
758	
759	It is worth noting that the current design is limited to a
760	\texttt{AIE\_SWITCHES} value of 1. Future work aims to increase this number
761	(see Section~\ref{sec:dma_strd_ctlr_pl_kern_improve} for more information). In
762	order for this PL kernel to be integrated into the Vivado design and a complete
763	XSA file be generated, the Vitis toolchain requires a system.cfg file that
764	specifies how the PL kernel is connected to the rest of the system. Prior to
765	the PL kernel being built, the Makefile will automatically update this
766	\textit{design/system\_cfg/system.cfg} file based on how the design is
767	configured within the \textit{design/common.h}.
768	
769	% =============================================================================
770	\subsection{AI Engine Graph Implementation}
771	% =============================================================================
772	\label{subsec:graph_impl}
773	
774	An AI Engine design must include a dataflow graph that guides the AI Engine
775	compiler in interconnecting kernels internally and linking them to external
776	domains within the Versal chip. For more information on AI Engine graphs, see
777	Section \ref{subsec:aie_graphs}.
778	
779	The general flow of data originates from the ARM processor. The ARM processor
780	provides the range compressed samples and the slow time data, which consists of
781	the antenna X, Y, and Z coordinates, as well as the range to target scene from
782	the antenna. In order to reduce the number of GMIO inputs being used (max of
783	32), all slow time data is sent through the same GMIO input port. The graph is
784	configured to forward this data to the Data Broadcast kernel and that graph
785	code is written to broadcast the Data Broadcast kernel output to all Image
786	Reconstruction kernels. \textit{Vitis Analyzer} was used to generate a block
787	diagram of the designed AI Engine graph, which can be seen in
788	Figure~\ref{fig:aie_graph} and \ref{fig:aie_graph_w_stride_ctl}.
789
